title: An individual based modelling approach to simulating Atlantic salmon post smolt migration in the Gulf of St. Lawrence
content:
Abstract
Understanding the early marine migration of Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) post-smolts is essential for conservation and management, particularly under changing ocean conditions. We developed a spatially explicit individual based model (IBM) to simulate post-smolt migration through the Gulf of St. Lawrence (GoSL), incorporating physical-biogeochemical ocean model output with candidate behavioural strategies. Simulated particles represented post-smolts navigating currents, temperature gradients, and prey fields, with behaviour informed by hypotheses of magnetic orientation and temperature-mediated movement. Model performance was validated against acoustic telemetry data from 511 smolts tagged in five southern GoSL rivers between 2007 and 2018. The most accurate simulations combined directed movement toward a target destination (Strait of Belle Isle) with mesozooplankton-seeking behaviour, mediated by thermal conditions (optimal range: 4–10 °C) and a swim speed of 2.5 body lengths per second. This modelled behavioural strategy outperformed others, including temperature directed and rheotaxis, in both arrival success and timing. Results suggest that post-smolts integrate multiple sensory and environmental cues to optimize migration timing and foraging. This approach enhances our understanding of salmon migration ecology and provides a flexible framework to explore how warming oceans and altered prey distributions may influence the migratory patterns of post-smolt.
